items.stem: Read Source D carefully. “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.” (Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948.) What can you infer from Source D about the ideas behind human rights?
items.answer: Human rights are based on the idea that every person has equal worth and that people have a duty to treat each other well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: Study Source B, Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948. “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. (b) Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Human rights are based on the idea that every person has equal worth and that people have a duty to treat each other well. (b) To set out a shared principle for all nations after the horrors of the Second World War.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: Scenario: Citizens of one ethnic group are not allowed to vote in national elections. (a) Suggest two actions that individuals or organisations could take in response. (b) Explain one reason why it can be difficult to protect this right in practice.
items.answer: (a) Report it to the media or a human rights NGO (e.g. Amnesty International); take a case to court or a national human rights commission; start a petition or peaceful campaign; contact elected representatives. (b) The government itself may be responsible; courts may not be independent; the UDHR is not directly enforceable; victims may fear reprisals or lack money for legal help.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Explain why human rights are described as “universal”.
items.answer: They belong to every person equally, everywhere in the world, regardless of nationality, gender, race, religion or any other status.
items.markingKey: 1 mark everyone; 1 mark regardless of status [2]

items.stem: Explain why rights come with responsibilities.
items.answer: If everyone has rights, each person has a duty to respect others’ rights – e.g. freedom of expression does not include the right to threaten or spread hatred about others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Scenario: A family is forced to leave their home and live on the street with no help. (a) Identify the human right that is being denied. (b) Suggest two actions that individuals or organisations could take in response.
items.answer: (a) The right to an adequate standard of living, including housing (UDHR Article 25). (b) Report it to the media or a human rights NGO (e.g. Amnesty International); take a case to court or a national human rights commission; start a petition or peaceful campaign; contact elected representatives.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark right [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has been successful in protecting human rights around the world. You may wish to consider: campaigners; enforcement.
items.answer: Agree: It set a global standard and inspired binding treaties, national constitutions and courts. Campaigners and NGOs such as Amnesty International use it to expose abuses. Disagree: It is not legally binding; many governments still use torture, censorship and discrimination. Genocides, e.g. Rwanda 1994, happened despite it. Rights are often unequal in practice, e.g. access to education. Judgement: It has been very influential in setting standards, but protection depends on governments and enforcement.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: How far do you agree that free elections are the most important feature of a democracy? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
items.answer: Agree: Elections give citizens the power to choose and remove leaders peacefully. Disagree: Without the rule of law, a free press and independent courts, elections can be manipulated and rights abused. Protection of minorities matters so the majority cannot oppress others. Judgement: Free elections are essential but not sufficient; democracy depends on a set of institutions working together.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “First-past-the-post is a fair way to elect a government.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: vote share and seats; simplicity; small parties.
items.answer: Agree: It is simple, links each MP to a constituency and usually gives a clear result. Disagree: Parties can win a majority of seats with a minority of votes. Smaller parties are under-represented. Proportional systems match seats more closely to votes. Judgement: It is effective at producing stable governments but less fair in representing voters’ choices.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A group of students in Lisbon is campaigning for protecting a local woodland from development. In two weeks their petition has collected 250 signatures in a community of about 5 000 people. Explain why collecting evidence would make the campaign more persuasive.

items.stem: A group of students in Madrid is campaigning for more recycling bins in the town centre. In two weeks their petition has collected 120 signatures in a community of about 2 000 people. items.answer: (a) 6% (b) The local council or school leadership (decision-makers), because they have the power and budget to make the change; also local media to raise awareness.

items.stem: Elena argues that peaceful protest is the most effective way for citizens to bring about change. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: protest and boycotts; legal action.
items.answer: Agree: Peaceful campaigns win public sympathy and media attention: the Montgomery bus boycott, Gandhi’s Salt March, Fridays for Future. Disagree: Voting and elections change governments and laws directly. Lobbying, petitions and legal challenges can achieve change quietly. Some groups (e.g. some suffragettes) argued militant action was needed when peaceful methods were ignored. Judgement: Peaceful protest is powerful, especially combined with voting, lobbying and legal action.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain two ways young people can be active citizens before they are old enough to vote.
items.answer: Join a school council or youth parliament; volunteer in the community; sign or start petitions; write to elected representatives; take part in peaceful campaigns or awareness projects.

items.stem: “Young people today have more power to make change than ever before.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: voting age; examples of youth campaigns; social media.
items.answer: Agree: Social media lets young people organise globally (school climate strikes from 2018). Youth parliaments and votes at 16 in some countries. Disagree: Many young people cannot vote and have little money or influence. Online campaigns may not lead to real change; decision-makers may ignore them. Young people in the past also led major movements. Judgement: Young people have new tools and reach, but turning attention into change still depends on political systems.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the qualities, beliefs, background and relationships that make a person who they are”.
items.answer: Identity
items.markingKey: Identity: the qualities, beliefs, background and relationships that make a person who they are. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the idea that a person belongs to several groups at once, such as a nationality, religion, family and local community”.
items.answer: Multiple identities
items.markingKey: Multiple identities: the idea that a person belongs to several groups at once, such as a nationality, religion, family and local community. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a person’s identity can change over time.
items.answer: People gain new experiences, move to new places, learn languages, change jobs or beliefs and join new groups, so how they see themselves – and which identity matters most – can change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark change factor; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: A survey of 100 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 41, “A little” 30, “Not at all” 29. Suggest two actions the local council could take to increase belonging.
items.answer: Community festivals and events; language classes; youth clubs and sports; involving residents in decisions; tackling discrimination.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that national identity is the most important part of who a person is. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: Nationality shapes language, culture, rights and how others see us. Disagree: Family, religion, ethnicity, local community, gender and interests may matter more to many people. Migrants and people with mixed heritage may have several national identities. Identity changes over time and in different situations. Judgement: National identity is important for many people, but identity is personal and made up of many parts.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the range of differences between people in a community, such as ethnicity, religion, language and culture”.
items.answer: Diversity
items.markingKey: Diversity: the range of differences between people in a community, such as ethnicity, religion, language and culture. [1]

items.stem: A survey of 100 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 59, “A little” 23, “Not at all” 18. (a) Calculate the percentage who answered “Not at all”. (b) Suggest two reasons why some residents may not feel they belong.
items.answer: (a) 18% (b) They may have recently arrived, face language barriers or discrimination, have few local friends or family, or feel excluded from local decisions.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “applying to everyone, everywhere, regardless of who they are”.

items.stem: A student writes: “Human rights only apply to adults.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Explain why the UDHR is important even though it is not a binding treaty.

items.stem: Scenario: A student is punished at school for practising her religion. Explain why this is a violation of human rights.
items.answer: Everyone is entitled to this right equally; the action treats the person as having less dignity and denies a freedom the UDHR says is universal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link to scenario; 1 mark universality/equality [2]

items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain two benefits of living in a diverse community.
items.answer: Learning about different cultures, foods, languages and festivals; wider range of skills and ideas for the economy; greater tolerance and understanding.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each [4]

items.stem: A survey of 120 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 61, “A little” 31, “Not at all” 28. Suggest two reasons why some residents may not feel they belong.
items.answer: They may have recently arrived, face language barriers or discrimination, have few local friends or family, or feel excluded from local decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the document of 30 articles adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 setting out rights for all people”.
items.answer: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
items.markingKey: Universal Declaration of Human Rights: the document of 30 articles adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 setting out rights for all people. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Governments can never limit any right in any circumstances.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Some rights (such as freedom from torture) are absolute, but others can be limited by law to protect others, e.g. for public safety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how two rights can come into conflict, with an example.
items.answer: E.g. freedom of expression (Article 19) can conflict with the right to privacy when newspapers publish private details; or freedom of assembly can conflict with others’ security. Courts must balance them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark two rights; 1 mark example; 1 mark balance [3]

items.stem: Scenario: A factory pays women less than men for exactly the same job. Suggest two actions that individuals or organisations could take in response.
items.answer: Report it to the media or a human rights NGO (e.g. Amnesty International); take a case to court or a national human rights commission; start a petition or peaceful campaign; contact elected representatives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study Source C, Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948. “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.” What can you infer from Source C about the ideas behind human rights?
items.answer: Human rights are based on the idea that every person has equal worth and that people have a duty to treat each other well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: “Responsibilities are just as important as rights.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: government duties; the law; respecting others.
items.answer: Agree: Rights only work if people respect the rights of others. Citizens’ responsibilities (obeying laws, voting, paying taxes) keep society functioning. Disagree: Human rights are inalienable – people should not lose them for failing a responsibility. Governments’ responsibility to protect rights matters most. Judgement: Rights and responsibilities depend on each other, but basic human rights should not be conditional.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has been successful in protecting human rights around the world.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: campaigners; influence on laws; continuing abuses.
items.answer: Agree: It set a global standard and inspired binding treaties, national constitutions and courts. Campaigners and NGOs such as Amnesty International use it to expose abuses. Disagree: It is not legally binding; many governments still use torture, censorship and discrimination. Genocides, e.g. Rwanda 1994, happened despite it. Rights are often unequal in practice, e.g. access to education. Judgement: It has been very influential in setting standards, but protection depends on governments and enforcement.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a system in which citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf”.
items.answer: Representative democracy
items.markingKey: Representative democracy: a system in which citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf. [1]

items.stem: Explain why an independent judiciary is important for the rule of law.
items.answer: Judges who are free from government control can apply the law fairly and rule against the government when it breaks the law, protecting citizens’ rights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark independence; 1 mark protects rights/holds government to account [2]

items.stem: Results in five constituencies (votes for Reform Alliance, Workers’ Party, Green Party): C1: 6023, 3544, 7117; C2: 8195, 3096, 6609; C3: 6056, 3640, 3781; C4: 5760, 5086, 4818; C5: 4726, 2143, 3687. The election uses first-past-the-post. Work out how many seats each party wins.
items.answer: Reform Alliance 4, Workers’ Party 0, Green Party 1
items.markingKey: winner = most votes in each constituency [2]

items.stem: Results in five constituencies (votes for Green Party, Reform Alliance, People’s Party): C1: 4319, 8487, 2050; C2: 3198, 8430, 3836; C3: 2236, 2232, 2684; C4: 8335, 4898, 3513; C5: 2307, 8188, 6129. The election uses first-past-the-post. (a) Constituency C1 has 50 000 registered voters. Calculate the turnout. (b) Suggest two reasons why turnout in elections may be low.
items.answer: (a) 29.7% (b) Voters feel their vote will not change the result (safe seats); distrust of politicians; difficulty getting to polling stations; lack of interest or information.

items.stem: “First-past-the-post is a fair way to elect a government.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: strong government; small parties.
items.answer: Agree: It is simple, links each MP to a constituency and usually gives a clear result. Disagree: Parties can win a majority of seats with a minority of votes. Smaller parties are under-represented. Proportional systems match seats more closely to votes. Judgement: It is effective at producing stable governments but less fair in representing voters’ choices.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “pressure group”?
options: Giving time and effort without pay to help others or the community.
An organisation that tries to influence government decisions without standing for election.
A non-profit organisation independent of government, such as Amnesty International or Oxfam.
A formal written request signed by many people and sent to those in power.
items.answer: An organisation that tries to influence government decisions without standing for election.
items.markingKey: Pressure group: an organisation that tries to influence government decisions without standing for election. [1]

items.stem: Explain why some campaigns succeed while others fail.
items.answer: Success depends on clear aims, wide public support, effective leadership, media attention, peaceful methods that win sympathy, and whether decision-makers are willing or able to respond.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor up to [3]

items.stem: A group of students in Istanbul is campaigning for free bus passes for students. In two weeks their petition has collected 600 signatures in a community of about 1 500 people. Explain why collecting evidence would make the campaign more persuasive.
items.answer: Data such as surveys or counts shows the problem is real and how many people it affects, so decision-makers are more likely to act.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shows need; 1 mark persuades decision-makers [2]

items.stem: A group of students in Seoul is campaigning for better lighting in the local park. In two weeks their petition has collected 250 signatures in a community of about 3 000 people. (a) Calculate the percentage of the community who have signed. (b) Identify who the students should try to persuade, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 8.3% (b) The local council or school leadership (decision-makers), because they have the power and budget to make the change; also local media to raise awareness.
items.markingKey: (a) 250 ÷ 3000 × 100 [1] (b) 1 mark target; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that young people today have more power to make change than ever before. You may wish to consider: voting age; social media; examples of youth campaigns.
items.answer: Agree: Social media lets young people organise globally (school climate strikes from 2018). Youth parliaments and votes at 16 in some countries. Disagree: Many young people cannot vote and have little money or influence. Online campaigns may not lead to real change; decision-makers may ignore them. Young people in the past also led major movements. Judgement: Young people have new tools and reach, but turning attention into change still depends on political systems.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Diversity always weakens a community.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many diverse communities are strong and cohesive; diversity brings new skills and ideas when people are included and treated fairly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways a community can help newcomers feel that they belong.
items.answer: Welcome events and clubs; language classes; inclusive festivals celebrating different cultures; mentoring or buddy schemes; making services available in several languages.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each [4]

items.stem: A survey of 100 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 42, “A little” 22, “Not at all” 36. Explain one limitation of this survey.
items.answer: A small sample may not represent the whole neighbourhood; people may not answer honestly; “belonging” means different things to different people; who was asked and where may bias results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation [2]
